case_name: Stanley v. KCL West Holdings Inc. et al
text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Stanley
v. KCL West Holdings Inc. et al,

2004
BCSC 1555

Date: 20041220

Docket: S074174

Registry: New Westminster

Between:

Scott Stanley

Plaintiff

And

KCL
West Holdings Inc. and

Denis Lehoux

Defendants

Before: Master Keighley

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel
for Plaintiff:

J.J. Casey

Counsel
for Defendants:

S. Mitchell

Date
and Place of Trial/Hearing:

October 28, 2004

New Westminster, B.C.

[
1
]

The plaintiff
seeks damages against his former employer, KCL West Holdings Inc. (“KCL”) for
breach of contract of employment and constructive dismissal.  Against his
former supervisor Denis Lehoux (“Lehoux”) and KCL he seeks damages for
intentional infliction of mental suffering and conspiracy.

[
2
]

The defendants
deny the plaintiff’s claims and counterclaim for damages arising out of the
plaintiff’s resignation.

APPLICATIONS

[
3
]

The plaintiff
applies under Rule 19(24)(a),(b) and (d) for orders that:

a)   paragraphs 8, 16 and 23 of the Statement of Defence and
Counterclaim be struck on the basis that they disclose no reasonable defence
and are unnecessary, frivolous or vexatious; and

b)   the Counterclaim be struck out on the grounds that it fails
to disclose a reasonable claim against the plaintiff, is unnecessary, frivolous
or vexatious and is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court.

[
4
]

The defendants
apply for orders under Rule 19 that:

a)   The allegations against Lehoux be struck out on the basis
that no reasonable claim against him has been disclosed in the Statement of Claim
and that the pleadings are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous and vexatious and
an abuse of the process of the court; and

b)   Paragraphs 16, 17, 21, 25, 26 and 27 be struck on the same
basis.

RULE
19(24)

[
5
]

Rule 19(24)
reads as follows:

“(24)
Scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious matters
– At any stage of a proceeding the court may
order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an endorsement,
pleading, petition or other document of the ground that:

(a)  it
discloses no reasonable claim or defence as the case may be,

(b)  it
is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious;

(c)  it
may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of the proceedings,
or

(d)  it
is otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the
court may grant judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and
may order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.”

[
6
]

In considering
applications under Rule 19(24) (a), the court proceeds on the assumption that
the facts alleged can be proven.  The applicant must show that it is “plain and
obvious” that the claim, as it stands or is amended, discloses no reasonable
cause of action or “no question fit to be tried”,
Hunt v. Carey Canada
Inc.

(1990)
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
,
49 B.C.L.R. (2d) 273 (S.C.C.)
at p. 289
.  Any doubt should
be resolved in favour of allowing the pleading to stand.  That a case is weak
or not likely to succeed is not a sufficient ground to strike it,
Minnes
v. Minnes

(1962)
1962 CanLII 350 (BC CA)
,
39 W.W.R. 112 (B.C.C.A.)

[
7
]

To succeed on
applications under Rule 19 (24) (b) and (d), the applicant must establish that
it is “plain and obvious” that the pleading offends either or both sub-rules,
Citizens
for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress

1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
,
[1999] B.C.J.
No. 2160 (S.C.)
,
347202 B.C. Ltd v. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce

[1995] B.C,J, No. 449 (S.C.)
.  Although the authorities provide little guidance
as to what constitutes a pleading which is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous,
and vexatious or otherwise an abuse of process, the following principles have
emerged: Bare prolixity will not be sufficient to order that a pleading be
struck.  Irrelevancy and embarrassment are established when pleadings are so
confusing that it is difficult, if not impossible, to understand them.  A
scandalous allegation will not be struck if it is relevant:
347202 B.C.
Ltd.
supra.  A pleading may be said to be vexatious “where it is
obvious that an action cannot succeed, or if the action would lead to no
possible good, or if no reasonable person can reasonably expect to obtain
relief”:
Ebrahim v. Ebrahim
[2002] B.C.J. No. 338 (C.A.)
.

THE PLAINTIFF’S APPLICATION

[
8
]

Paragraphs 8,
16 and 23 of the Statement of Defence and Counterclaim read as follows:

8.   In further answer to the whole of the Statement of Claim,
the plaintiff knew of the defendant KCL’s intention to close the Port Coquitlam
head office and later of the intention to give the employees, including the
plaintiff, working notice, and he acted in an insubordinate and inappropriate
manner to the defendant Denis Lehoux (“Lehoux”) with the specific intent of
resigning and alleging constructive dismissal so that he could avoid being
given working notice and obtain a severance package.

16.  In further and alternative answer to the whole of the
Statement of Claim, the plaintiff has named the defendant Lehoux personally in
a malicious attempt to cause harm to Lehoux and with the knowledge that Lehoux
had acted appropriately and within the scope of his employment duties and
responsibilities. The conduct of the plaintiff was malicious, highhanded and
reckless and constitutes an abuse of process.

23.  In further answer to the whole of the Statement of Claim,
the plaintiff’s premature resignation and plan to allege constructive dismissal
when there was no such constructive dismissal has caused the defendants to
suffer damage.  Particulars include:

a)   the defendant KCL was required to retain consultants to
complete projects which the plaintiff was to have completed;

b)   the defendant KCL was required to ship personnel boxes to
the Edmonton, Alberta office unexpectedly;

c)   the defendant KCL was
required to purchase several plane tickets to travel to the Port Coquitlam
office to look after matters which were the responsibility of the plaintiff;
and

d)   the defendant KCL was required to find other employees who
could work additional hours on projects that should have or would have been
completed by the plaintiff.

The defendants will seek to set
off these damages against any damages owing to the plaintiff.

[
9
]

The
Counterclaim reads as follows:

1.   The defendants repeat the allegations set out in the
Statement of Defence.

2.   As a result of the plaintiff’s conduct the defendants have
sustained damages, particulars of which are set out in paragraph 22 (sic) of
the Statement of Defence.

3.   By reason of the tortuous conduct of the plaintiff to the
defendant Lehoux, Lehoux’s reputation has been damaged and he has suffered
damages, loss and expense.

The defendants claim as follows:

a)   general damages;

b)   aggravated damages;

c)   punitive damages;

d)   special costs, and

e)   such further and other relief as this Honourable Court may
deem just.

[
10
]

The plaintiff
says that, even if the allegations contained in paragraph 8 of the Statement of
Defence and Counterclaim are true, they do not amount to a substantive defence
to his claim.  The essence of the defence must be, he says, that the plaintiff
resigned voluntarily.  As such the allegations in paragraph 8 are not
necessary

in furtherance of the defence.  The defendants say that paragraph 8 alleges
facts which establish the plaintiff’s improper purpose in attempting to
characterize his resignation as constructive dismissal in order to receive
severance and cause harm to Lehoux.  I am mindful of the wording of Rule 19 (1)
which provides, in part:

“A pleading . . . must contain a statement in summary
form of the facts on which the party relies, but not the evidence by which the
facts are to be proved.”

[
11
]

I am unable to
say that the pleading in paragraph 8 is unnecessary on the basis of the “plain
and obvious” test.  The issue of the plaintiff’s motivation to resign will, no
doubt, be a significant issue in this litigation.  Accordingly, the plaintiff’s
application to strike paragraph 8 is dismissed.

[
12
]

Similarly, the
plaintiff says that the allegations contained in paragraph 16 do not amount to
a substantive defence to the plaintiff’s claim.  He says that the appropriate
remedy for a plea of abuse of process is an application for a judicial stay of
proceedings and refers to the decision of Macaulay, J. in the case of
Lasik
Vision Canada Inc. v. TLC Vancouver Optometric Group Inc.
[2000] B.C.J.
No. 1639
, in which the learned judge, at paragraph 4 said:

“There is no question that the court has the
jurisdiction to stay proceedings that are an abuse of process. However, an
abuse of process rarely constitutes an independent cause of action on which a
party may sue and does not, on any authority brought to my attention, give rise
to a substantive defence to be raised in response to a claim. Instead, where
the commencement of an action is an abuse of process, the remedy available to a
defendant is a judicial stay of proceedings.”

[
13
]

The defendants
have referred me to the decisions of this Court and our Court of Appeal,
respectively, in
Starbucks Corp v. Second Cup Ltd et al

(1993)
1993 CanLII 1300 (BC SC)
,
46
C.P.R. (3d) 492
and
Border Enterprises Ltd. V. Beazer East, Inc.

[2002] B.C.J. No. 1829
.  These authorities establish the proposition that there
exists a separate tort of abuse of process.  In both cases, claims were made,
rather than defences raised, on the basis on abuse of process allegations.
Neither case suggests that abuse of process allegations may form the basis of a
defence, as such.  The
Starbucks
case considered whether the
facts supporting an abuse of process claim, raised by way of counterclaim,
could arise out of the lawsuit itself (as is alleged by this pleading), and
left that issue for determination by the trial judge.  An amendment may be
necessary to bring this issue before the court but, at present, the issue is
improperly raised by way of defence.  Accordingly, paragraph 16 of the
Statement of Defence and Counterclaim will be struck.

[
14
]

In support of
his application to strike paragraph 23 of the Statement of Defence and
Counterclaim, the plaintiff says that the pleading is based on the principle of
set-off.  It is plain and obvious, he says that the defence will fail as, if
the plaintiff is successful is establishing constructive dismissal there can be
no damages for premature resignation and if he is unsuccessful, there will be
nothing to set-off against.  The defendants have referred me to authorities in
support of the proposition that it is an implied term of any contract of
employment that an employee will give reasonable notice of termination and that
an employer may recover damages for business loss and expenses arising from the
failure to give proper notice:
RBC Dominion Securities Inc. v. Merrill
Lynch Canada
2003 BCSC 1773 (CanLII)
,
[2003] B.C.J. No. 2700 (S.C.)
,
Sure-Grip Fasteners
Ltd. v. Allgrade Bolt and Chain Inc.

(1993)
1993 CanLII 17526 (ON SC)
,
45 C.C.E.L. 276 (Ont. G.D.)

and
Lower Mainland Better Hearing Centres Inc. (c.o.b. Beltone Hearing
Centre) v. Zhang

[1996] B.C.J. No. 90
.  Again, these are claims which
may properly be advanced by way of Counterclaim.  They do not, in the
circumstances, amount to a defence.  Paragraph 23 will be struck in its
entirety.

[
15
]

The
Counterclaim is essentially based upon the allegations contained in paragraphs
16 and 23 of the Statement of Defence, both of which I have ordered struck.  I
am mindful, however, of Rule 1(5) which provides:

“The object of these rules is to secure the just, speedy
and inexpensive determination of every proceeding on its merits.”

[
16
]

In the
interest of ensuring that all issues are properly before the court at the
eventual trial of this matter, the defendants will have 30 days from the date
of entry of this order to make application to amend the Counterclaim.  This
aspect of the plaintiff’s application is adjourned generally with liberty to
the plaintiff to reschedule it for hearing following the expiration of this
30-day period.

THE DEFENDANTS’ APPLICATION

[
17
]

The
plaintiff’s claim against Lehoux is that he individually, or in collusion with
KCL, planned to cause the plaintiff to resign or, alternatively, to establish
“trumped-up” grounds for dismissal.

[
18
]

Following the
preliminary averments, the plaintiff’s allegations concerning Lehoux are,
essentially, as follows:

a)   On February 1, 1995, the plaintiff began employment with a
company which eventually came to be operated by KCL;

b)   In April 1996, the plaintiff was promoted to the position
of Quality Assurance Manager;

c)   In January 1997, the plaintiff was promoted to the position
of Employee Development Manager;

d)   In December 2001, the plaintiff became an employee of KCL
in the same capacity;

e)   At that time, KCL indicated that it was relocating its head
office to Edmonton and invited the plaintiff to relocate there.  The plaintiff
declined, in the belief that he could continue in the same role at the Port
Coquitlam branch;

f)   On January 28, 2002, KCL hired Lehoux as General
Manager-Human Resources in Edmonton;

g)   Commencing in or about mid-February 2002, Lehoux, either
alone or in concert with KCL embarked on a plan to cause the plaintiff to
resign or build grounds for dismissal.  Lehoux, with intent to inflict mental
distress on the plaintiff, subjected him to personal attacks concerning his
abilities, performance and character, created a hostile and intimidating
working environment, accused the plaintiff if insubordination and attempts to
undermine Lehoux’s authority, excluded the plaintiff from participating in
policy development, harassed the plaintiff over his refusal to relocate to
Edmonton, conducted himself in a manner calculated to undermine the plaintiff’s
confidence and self-esteem and conducted himself in a manner calculated to
embarrass and humiliate the plaintiff amongst other KCL employees;

h)   On April 19, 2002, Lehoux told the plaintiff that there was
no human resources job for him in British Columbia and that his refusal to move
to Edmonton was notice of his resignation;

i)   On April 21, 2002, the plaintiff tendered his resignation;

j)   As a result of Lehoux’s conduct and KCL’s breach of the
contract of employment, the plaintiff has suffered mental stress and emotional
anxiety, embarrassment and humiliation, loss of self-esteem and self-worth,
loss of income and impairment of his ability to locate alternate employment.

[
19
]

The defendants
say that, in order to establish a cause of action against an employee of a
corporation, a plaintiff must establish that the individual committed a tortious
act which demonstrated an identity or interest, separate from that of the
corporation:
Dorus v. Teck Corp

[2002] B.C.J. No. 751
,
Morriss
v. British Columbia

[2001] B.C.J. No. 369
,
Napoleone v. Baraldi

[2004] B.C.J. No 1653
.

[
20
]

While there is
no specific allegation in the Statement of Claim to the effect that Lehoux
acted outside the scope of his corporate authority (in fact, there is an
alternative claim alleging vicarious liability on the part of the employer)
there are allegations of conduct which, surely, would not be sanctioned by any
reasonable employer, such as those alleging personal attacks by Lehoux, his
creation of an intimidating, hostile environment, his harassment of the
plaintiff over the plaintiff’s refusal to relocate and the more vague
allegations of behaviour calculated to embarrass and humiliate the plaintiff
and undermine his confidence and self-esteem.  I must assume, for the purposes
of this application, that these allegations can be proven.  In the issue of
whether Lehoux might be liable to the plaintiff for damages for the intentional
infliction of mental suffering, I cannot say that it is “plain and obvious”
that there is no claim against Lehoux fit to be tried.  Accordingly, the
defendants’ application to strike those portions of the claim as against Lehoux
is dismissed.

[
21
]

The defendants
also seek to strike those portions of the Statement of Claim alleging
conspiracy.  I will say, first of all, that I have difficulty with the notion
that Lehoux and KCL could conspire to wrongfully terminate the plaintiff’s
employment.  The company, and the company alone, had the authority to hire or
fire and even in the event that Lehoux and KCL agreed to work jointly to
procure the plaintiff’s resignation, Lehoux would have been acting in his
capacity as an employee.  If the act of termination then becomes the act of the
employer alone, it cannot be said to conspire with itself and it would then be
“plain and obvious” that this aspect of the claim is bound to fail.  I note
Master Joyce (as he then was) followed similar reasoning in the case of
Khun
v. American Indemnity Co.

[1992] B.C.J. No. 953
, in arriving at a
similar conclusion.

[
22
]

There is,
however, another aspect to the plaintiff’s claim, that of intentional
infliction of mental suffering.  With respect to this ground for relief, which
one would expect would arise outside of the contract of employment, it is
theoretically possible for the employer to conspire with an employee to induce
suffering in another employee, although it is difficult to imagine how this would
not result in the employer assuming sole responsibility for the claim.  This is
particularly so when the claim, as here, does not differentiate between the
claim for wrongful dismissal and the claim for intentional infliction of mental
suffering.  In paragraph 16 of the Statement of Claim, the plaintiff refers to
a plan “calculated to cause the plaintiff to resign from his employment, or
alternatively, to build trumped-up grounds for his dismissal”.  The plaintiff
refers to this arrangement as the “Plan”.  Paragraph 17 sets out the manner in

which
Lehoux “pursuant to the Plan” set out to undermine and discredit the
plaintiff.  Nothing further is pleaded by way of facts which would support the
conclusion, reached in paragraph 25 that “the conduct of KCL was malicious and
in complete disregard of the plaintiff’s rights”, unless, that is the employer
was liable for the acts of its employee.

[
23
]

It appears
that amendments are required to clarify whether the conspiracy alleged is as to
termination (and I have already expressed my reservations with respect to such
a claim) or as to the tort of intentional infliction of mental suffering, in
which case facts must be pleaded to support KCL’s liability independent of any
liability it may have pursuant to the principle of vicarious liability.  The
plaintiff will have 30 days from the date of entry of this order to amend.  The
defendants’ application to strike those portions of the Statement of Claim
dealing with conspiracy will be adjourned generally with liberty to the defendants
to revisit the issue following amendment or expiration of this period.

[
24
]

Each party
will bear his/their own costs.

“Master P. Keighley”
